messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

James, a thirty-year-old carpenter, still cannot find the words for what happened that afternoon in the workshop. He was steadying a length of oak while his colleague, Mike, ran the table saw. The blade caught a knot; the wood kicked back. Mike’s hand slid forward into the spinning blade. James saw the fingers separate, saw the blood spray across the bench, felt the warm wetness on his own face and hands. He tried to clamp a towel around Mike’s wrist, and for a moment the metallic taste of blood—his own or Mike’s, he could never sort out—filled his mouth. That taste, the slick of blood on his palms, the image of Mike’s ruined hand: these are the pieces that have shattered his life.

Months later, any physical touch can drop him back into that moment. When his wife places a hand on his shoulder, he flinches. The pressure of sawdust against his skin on a job site makes his stomach lurch. And each time that happens, the full memory returns without warning—not as a recollection but as a complete sensory reliving: the scream, the spray, the taste, the sticky heat on his hands. It all comes back at once, and he cannot put any of it into words. He has tried to tell his wife what it feels like, but the words dissolve. So instead, when the memory hits, he does everything he can to shut it down. He deliberately tries to leave his body, focusing on a spot on the ceiling until he blanks out. Or he eats—cookies, sandwiches, anything—to fill the hollow that opens in his chest. He has come to believe that his life has been permanently destroyed, that he is fundamentally changed for the worse and can no longer rely on himself to stay present or to protect anyone.

The taste itself has become a trap. If he catches even a hint of metal in his mouth—from a fork, from the air after rain—the reliving begins again, and with it the conviction that he is damaged beyond repair. And that conviction, in turn, makes him hypervigilant to every possible trigger. He scans his environment for signs of injury, avoids touching raw materials with his bare hands, and recoils from his wife’s affection because the appraisals of permanent change make him believe that any sensory reminder will confirm he is ruined. The cycle tightens: a trigger brings the memory; the memory reinforces his negative beliefs; those beliefs make him more sensitive to triggers; and each maladaptive response—the overeating, the dissociation, the refusal to think about the event—only deepens his sense that he has lost control of his life.

At work, he can no longer handle jobs that require close teamwork. He turned down a kitchen renovation because it meant working near a saw. His marriage has grown strained; his wife feels pushed away, and he cannot explain why he flinches from her. He has started avoiding thinking about the accident altogether, but the thoughts break through anyway, unbidden. Last week, while sanding a cabinet, a splinter drew a bead of blood on his thumb. The taste of copper flooded his mouth, and he was back in the workshop, hands slick, Mike’s scream in his ears, the belief that his life is over solidifying once more. That was when he finally called a clinic.

He is not sure what help could look like. He is certain he can never go back to who he was, and he is terrified that talking will make it worse. But he cannot go on like this—every touch a warning, every taste a trap, every working day a fresh confrontation with his own brokenness.

violation_explanations: No paragraph directly shows that triggers lead to maladaptive strategies; triggers instead lead to memory or negative appraisals which then prompt strategies.
No paragraph directly shows that triggers cause negative appraisals; the link goes through memory (trigger → memory → appraisal).
No paragraph directly shows that negative appraisals cause intrusive memories; memories are triggered by external cues and then reinforce appraisals.
No paragraph directly shows that memory causes triggers; memory increases sensitivity to triggers via appraisals, not directly.
